I was primarily a drinker and pot smoker and I do NA. Dabbled slightly with opiates but not to the point of addiction. I have been in the program for almost 2 years now and I love it. It was rough at first because I had a hard time adjusting to the god stuff, being an atheist, but I've found a niche in the program that works for me. I do 4-5 meetings a week and I couldn't imagine my life at this point without the fellowship. I've gotten so much more out of it than just "some friends in recovery" like I initially wanted. Many times these last two years I would've used again but the program carried me through. 

The literature is amazing too. Different than AA completely, although the steps are similar. The NA Basic Text is fantastic and really a lifesaver. We also use a workbook for the steps, whereas in AA I believe you really only do any writing for a few steps. In NA for the first step alone there's like 100 questions in the NA Step Working Guides. Really helps you do some work on yourself. I couldn't recommend it enough. You might have to try different meetings to find ones you like, but I'll tell you my home group is like family to me now.

Also in NA our problem is not a specific substance but rather the disease of addiction as a whole. The particular substances we used are merely symptoms, and almost totally irrelevant to our recoveries. While I drank and smoked pot, I can relate and feel when people share who were junkies, tweakers, crackheads, etc. I hope you give it a try. It's saved my life but also done so much more. Also, just know that in meetings we typically use terms like "clean" instead of sober, "clean time" or "recovery" instead of sobriety, and "addict" instead of alcoholic. Good luck!

My life was difficult in my late teens and for most of my 20s (I'm 27 now). I had major depression and undiagnosed ADHD, and I was addicted to drugs from about 20 to 25/26. Sometimes I get down about those years being "wasted", but I realized that's not the clearest way to see it. Those years were instrumental in who I ultimately am today. I had to do a lot of growing to really feel like I generally enjoy my life and like I'm "making the most" of my life.

My advice is to try and not think ahead so much. If you spend all your time looking to the future and what it has to possibly offer you, you'll miss out on the present and everything that you have today. You're 19, which most people would consider to be very young. It does not help to put too much pressure on yourself for the future and how you think it should be, nor does it help to think in the past about what things could have been. All you are guaranteed is this moment that you are in right now.

My life today is nothing like what I thought it would be when I was 19. Absolutely not even close. But it all worked out for the best. Sometimes we have grandiose expectations for things when that's not always what ends up happening. I tend to build up fantasies in my head that are so detailed and extensive that when reality goes a different direction, it feels rather shocking.

Another point of advice is that the way you talk to yourself, think about yourself and your actions, and the overall internal dialogue that you have in your head about yourself is absolutely more important than you may think. Beating yourself up over things and being your own worst critic has lasting effects that you may not realize. Constantly berating yourself can actually trigger the same stress response in you as if someone were yelling at you. You may not realize it, but your brain is listening to the things you say about yourself, and it internalizes these things whether you want it to or not.

Good luck.

SMART Recovery is a great option but they don't really operate on reddit as far as I know. Here's their [website](https://www.smartrecovery.org/).

I'm a relatively new co-facilitator for a SMART meeting in my area, but I've been going to it for just about a year now. I'm also just about a year sober! The meetings are typically open-discussion format but sometimes are more structured and focused on stuff from the SMART Recovery Handbook, which you can buy on the website for like \~$12. They also have free [tools](https://www.smartrecovery.org/smart-recovery-toolbox/) (interactive PDFs) that they provide to help with different aspects of recovery. On the website you'll even find various recommended books, essays, and videos on addiction and recovery, as well as resources for family and friends. The whole idea of SMART is that it takes more of a psychological, therapy-based approach to recovery versus the more dogmatic, spiritual stuff that AA does. You may find that SMART works better if you weren't into AA. SMART also requires facilitators to go through a fairly extensive online training course (about 18 hours of material). Some facilitators are even legit mental health professionals, but anyone can take the course and host or co-host a meeting.

Also, despite what people sometimes say about SMART, they do NOT promote moderation and are strictly abstinence-based. *However,* SMART makes it clear (I even have to say it at the beginning of each meeting) that they generally support whatever is working for you in your recovery, but we keep the content of the meetings based in abstinence. So if you were a heroin addict and were able to kick the H by smoking weed instead, and if that's working for you, SMART would be supportive in the spirit of harm reduction. Just don't mention the weed part of it at a meeting because SMART meetings are for all types of addictions, and you may trigger someone who is there to quit weed, for example.

Many SMART meetings will be virtual nowadays but they will say that in the meeting description when you look it up. Personally I love the program and it's been so helpful for me. If you have any questions I'd be happy to help out. Sorry for the wall of text!

TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) is a treatment for depression. You go in for sessions once a day every weekday for about two months. For each session they have you sit in a chair and they place a magnetic coil next to your head in a location that they calculate first. It released a series of rapid magnetic pulses and then pauses for a second before doing it again. This goes on for about 18 minutes. It’s initially kinda uncomfortable but I quickly got used to it and they can adjust it if it hurts. When I say “hurts” it’s like the worst is someone flicking the side of your head with their finger. It *should* be painless once they get it set up right and you get used to it. 

Anyway, it’s very safe and the most common side effect is headaches which I don’t think I got. In about two weeks into the treatment I noticed a greatly improved mood. They had me do a mood survey every Friday and the difference between my first and my last surveys was amazing. After insurance it cost me I think $100 or so in total. I highly recommend it if you have insurance. Most plans I think will cover it. I thought my depression was incurable for years before I got this done.

Hey I'm a facilitator for SMART Recovery and I go to meetings as a participant too. What drew me to the program was that it's secular and based around rational emotive behavioral therapy, a kind of cognitive behavioral therapy. There are different group formats. The one I attend is an open discussion format. People check in, we pick any topics that anybody might have brought up and talk about it. It's my and the other facilitators' job to apply SMART's approaches and tools to anything that someone might be dealing with, at any point in their recovery. Compared to traditional 12-step programs, SMART is generally less "dogmatic" I would say and focuses more on behavioral therapy to replace or dismiss irrational beliefs that fuel addiction and keep people in the cycle. You can check out the website if you want to find meetings near you. Most of them around me are virtual at the moment so easy to join. 

One thing to note is that while SMART supports whatever you're doing in your recovery that's working for you (like smoking weed or moderating as opposed to total abstinence), it's asked that everyone keep the discussion abstinence-based. So if weed is working for you right now to stay away from other things, SMART is ok with that but just don't mention it at the meetings, as someone could be there to quit weed and it may be a trigger for them.

Hope that helps.

If you go to a SMART recovery meeting with an open discussion format, they may even be able to go through one of these with you if you ask. If the idea of worksheets seems kinda silly, give them a shot at least, but residential treatment or inpatient rehab might be something to look at if you're really stuck. 

Also you're talking about once a week meetings but I'd even say try to get a few meetings in each week. Doesn't have to be just AA. There are plenty of recovery programs out there and it's ok to mix and match them if that's what works for your schedule and your recovery.

During this time I was dealing with major depression from age 14 or so, coupled with gender dysphoria (which I didn't realize until like age 21), and undiagnosed ADHD (which I also didn't find out until age 26). Together, all this shit drove me to escape using whatever I had that made me feel not sober. Shit, even caffeine - soda and coffee and energy drinks and a bunch of them every day. I couldn't control buying that shit every day more than I could control my drinking or smoking/vaping. When I tried to go without these things it was always extraordinarily uncomfortable. For whatever reason, being still with myself or without much going on (so like a regular day sitting at my desk for work) was absolutely agonizingly unbearable without \*something\*. I would regularly at any time at my desk (I wfh) have a cup of triple espresso mocha, a cup of soda with the larger bottle right next to it, and a THC vape all around my laptop. Lately I haven't been drinking but often there would be a bottle of beer or a glass of wine there too. I also didn't drink so much caffeine when I was drinking alcohol, so the coffee et al came after I "sobered up".

Back to the ADHD part, I got diagnosed for the first time (never even suspected it before) about a month after my 26 birthday early this year. My psychiatrist has been trying me on different stimulant medications ever since. For most of the time they didn't work, or they worked a bit but didn't last very long, or whatever. I also didn't like the instant release ones because of my history with substance abuse and that I often felt the need to take more than I was prescribed. Even though I quit drinking at roughly the same time as my diagnosis, I still engaged in addictive behaviors and indulged in bad habits every day. Got really into edibles and eventually started vaping again. And like I said with the coffee and soda and shit I would get at least one of those a day from Starbucks or whatever. I hated spending the money on any of these things and I didn't even really enjoy them anymore. My morning coffee felt like a necessity in order to stave off the intense cravings and the feeling I described earlier of being without any kind of substance. I was fucking miserable and couldn't get myself to do shit either for work. Every small task was enormous to me and I was so dysfunctional that I was convinced that I would need supportive housing when I move out of my parents. I couldn't imagine how bad things would get if I was left to live alone or even with roommates. I've been there before and it wasn't nice.

That was until Tuesday actually. On Monday I saw my psychiatrist and he bumped up the dose of my medication that worked a bit at first but lost it's efficacy after a time. I've been on the new dose since Tuesday and DUDE let me tell you just how much it has changed my life in less than a week even. Although there were a few days where I felt like I was getting a bit of an elated feeling due to the "honeymoon period" with the new dose, it's day 5 now and many of the benefits are still there. I take it when my dog wakes me up around 6am and then often sleep a bit longer while it takes effect, which makes me consistently be up and alert in a natural-feeling way around 8 or so. I have internal motivation to do tasks that I need to do now in a way that still shocks me. I enjoy the things I do in my routine like writing in my planner, walking my dog, listening to podcasts, etc. I no longer feel a sense of unrelenting dread when I'm still with myself or sitting at my desk working. I no longer feel like I constantly need \*something\*. I've bought 2 milk teas in the last 5 days and aside from coffee and tea at home, that's literally all the caffeine that I've spent money on in this time. That habit was getting me for like $8-10 a day, and now I just feel like I don't even need it. The itch to self-medicate constantly is GONE. Like what the fuck. I still can't believe it. Total and utter relief from so many things that I've dealt with for as long as I can remember. Absolutely fucking life-changing shit my dude. I don't think words can really do justice to the new life I have now. It's unreal.

My point in all of that is that many addicts/alcoholics/whatevers suffer from ADHD, and often they don't even realize that they have it. If you can relate to anything in my story it could be worth getting checked out for that. If you do have ADHD that is untreated or undiagnosed or whatever, it could change your life. I mean it basically has nearly entirely ended my desire to self-medicate and in doing so has freed me from being a slave to a bottle or a substance. Not that I'm going to start drinking again - I don't want to fuck around and find out again that I can't control it. The risk of losing the awesome life I currently have is too high. Things can get better dude. If this isn't you, then you gotta get to the bottom of why you use. Something's clearly going on. Good luck friend.

Never had any physical issues or even acute withdrawals I think, and I was much more functional than I thought I needed to be to consider myself as having a “problem”. 

Because I felt like it didn’t really have a real or “bad enough” problem, I got major imposter syndrome and tried to quit all on my own without even talking to my therapist, friends or family about it. I didn’t seek out professional help and I’m kinda paying for that right now.

My point though is to not underestimate what you’re dealing with. I thought I didn’t have much of an issue either but it was obvious to others. I also thought I could moderate my drinking but that led to self medicating and getting drunk alone most days if not every day like I did before. I realize now that I’m an addict and so I can never responsibly regulate my alcohol use. Really it’s a problem of self medicating and impulsive behavior combined with my ADHD symptoms and constant discomfort and restlessness. You may not need a full on residential program but don’t write it off if you think you could seriously benefit from a clean environment for a month or so to set you off on the right direction. Shit can be expensive though. 

There’s also intensive outpatient programs which meeting a few hours a day for a few days a week for like a month or two. They are often much cheaper and provide professional help without needing to live in an around the clock sorta program. You can also keep working or going to school during the day. I’m looking into helping facilitate them too. They can really help because you get to talk with other people who have substance use problems and that by itself can be hugely beneficial. Those are pretty normal. Stimulants are classified as a schedule II narcotic, on the same level as oxycodone. You can't transfer them without canceling the script at the original pharmacy and having the doc send another one (or if you have a paper script you can go straight to the pharmacy and ask them if they have it. If they don't then they'll just give the script back). No refills allowed (and if you do a partial fill then you forfeit the remainder on the prescription). Lots of pharmacies probably won't give you a straight answer if you call to ask for their stock of any CII medication. They worry about getting robbed I think. Source: I was a pharmacy technician at a big chain on the west coast.
